Title: Doing Up Your Skates Wrong Is the First Beginner Problem
Description: Ask a certified coach for the most common problems in inline skating and the first one is not technique: skates that are not done up correctly. A loose boot cannot hold your ankle in line, and every drill after that fights the equipment. Before you blame balance, knees or ankles, check how tight the top of your skate is. Title: Inline Skate Buckles: Your Top Strap Jams Before It Is Tight
Description: Why you cannot get the top ankle strap tight, and it is not your hands: a one-centimetre fix. A certified coach names the buckle jam: a long plastic strap runs into the buckle housing and sticks before the cuff is snug. The fix is yours to do: trim about a centimetre off the end of the strap so it can travel further into the buckle. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Inline Skate Ankle Strap Test: Bend Until Your Knees Cover Your Toes
Description: A test for how tight the top ankle strap should be, instead of a feeling. Do the top strap up, then bend your knees until they cover your toes. The cuff should hold you at the deepest point of that bend without stopping the movement itself. If your ankle can still tilt inward down there, the strap is not doing its job yet. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Moving Your Frames Treats the Symptom, Not the Cause
Description: Whether moving your inline frames fixes ankles that collapse inward: usually it does not. A certified coach's answer: it usually comes from too little knee bend and knees drifting inward, not from where the frame sits. Move the frame first and the fault stays. Drive the knee forward and slightly out, over the little toe, instead. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Frame Shifts Come After Edge Control, Not Before
Description: The right time to move your frames is late. A certified coach only shifts them once a skater has conscious edge control and corrected posture errors. Who then benefits: skaters with an unusual natural stance, such as pigeon toes, or those on tall setups with very big wheels. Everyone else leaves the frame where the factory put it. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Frame Tweaks Are Millimetres, Never a Relocation
Description: When a frame shift is justified, it is small. A certified coach is precise: frame tweaks are micro-adjustments measured in millimetres, never an extreme repositioning. And moving frames is personal: what suits another skater's stance does not transfer to yours, so a shift is tested on your own one-foot glide, not copied from anyone. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Big Wheels Lift You Higher, and the Frame Position Matters More
Description: Big wheels can justify a small frame shift: they lift your foot much higher. A certified coach names these high-centre big-wheel setups among the few cases where a subtle frame shift can genuinely help. On a standard beginner setup, low to the ground, the same inward lean is a knee-bend problem first, and the frame stays where it is. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Rockered Inline Frames Are a Style, Not a Requirement
Description: Flat or rockered frames for wizard-style transitions: both work, differently. On a flat setup you flip the skate; on a rockered one you cusp, rolling through the curve. The rocker makes cusping easier and gives that swishy look, but it is not essential. Pick the frame for how you want to skate, not out of obligation. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: New Frames? Day One Is Basics, Not Tricks
Description: A certified coach does not test new frames on hard moves. She goes easy on first days with new equipment: revise the basics, check that the one-foot glide is not pronated and stays easy to hold and control with knee bend, then practise normal strides to feel whether all is in alignment. Only then do the complicated moves return. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Inline Skate Strap Over Your Tendon: It Is Not Too Tight
Description: Why the ankle strap hurts after ten minutes, and why it is not too tight. A certified coach points elsewhere: the angled strap sits over the tendon to your big toe. Stand tall, weight drops to your heels, the tendon pops up under the strap, and your toes grip until the arch cramps. Sink into knees over toes: the tendon relaxes. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
